notes.text: Very early in the morning, a great while before day. Jacob had helped his wives and children over the river, and he desired to be private, and was left alone, that he might again spread his cares and fears before God in prayer. While Jacob was earnest in prayer, stirring up himself to take hold on God, an angel takes hold on him. Some think this was a created angel, one of those that always behold the face of our Father. Rather it was the angel of the covenant, who often appeared in a human shape, before he assumed the human nature. We are told by the prophet, Hosea xii, 4, how Jacob wrestled, he wept and made supplication; prayers and tears were his weapons. It was not only a corporal, but a spiritual wrestling by vigourous faith and holy desire.

The angel prevailed not against him — That is, this discouragement did not shake his faith, nor silence his prayer. It was not in his own strength that he wrestled, nor by his own strength that he prevails; but by strength derived from heaven. That of Job illustrates this, Job xxiii, 6. Will he plead against me with his great power? No; had the angel done so, Jacob had been crushed; but he would put strength in me: and by that strength Jacob had power over the angel, Hosea xii, 3. The angel put out Jacob's thigh, to shew him what he could do, and that it was God he was wrestling with, for no man could disjoint his thigh with a touch. Some think that Jacob felt little or no pain from this hurt; it is probable be did not, for he did not so much as halt 'till the struggle was over, ver. 31, and if so, that was an evidence of a divine touch indeed, which wounded and healed at the same time.

Let me go — The angel, by an admirable condescension, speaks Jacob fair to let him go, as God said to Moses, Exod. xxxii, 10. Let me alone. Could not a mighty angel get clear of Jacob's grapples? He could; but thus he would put an honour upon Jacob's faith and prayer. The reason the angel gives why he would be gone is because the day breaks, and therefore he would not any longer detain Jacob, who had business to do, a journey to go, a family to look after. And he said, I will not let thee go except thou bless me - He resolves he will have a blessing, and rather shall all his bones be put out of joint, than he will go away without one. Those that would have the blessing of Christ must be in good earnest, and be importunate for it.

What is thy name? — Jacob (saith he) a supplanter, so Jacob signifies. Well, (faith the angel) be thou never so called any more: thou shalt be called Israel, a prince with God. He is a prince indeed, that is a prince with God; and those are truly honourable that are mighty, in prayer. Yet this was not all; having, power with God, he shall have power with men too; having prevailed for a blessing from heaven, he shall, no doubt, prevail for Esau's favour. Whatever enemies we have, if we can but make God our friend, we are well enough; they that by faith have power in heaven, have thereby as much power on earth as they have occasion for.

Wherefore dost thou ask after my name? — What good will it do thee to know that? The discovery of that was reserved for his death-bed, upon which he was taught to call him Shiloh. But instead of telling him his name, he gave him his blessing, which was the thing he wrestled for; he blessed him there, repeated and ratified the blessing formerly given him. See how wonderfully God condescends to countenance and crown importunate prayer? Those that resolve though God slay them, yet to trust in him, will at length be more than conquerors.
Peniel — That is, the face of God, because there he had seen the appearance of God, and obtained the favour of God.

He halted on his thigh — And some think he continued to do so to his dying day. If he did, he had no reason to complain, for the honour and comfort he obtained by his struggle was abundantly sufficient to countervail the damage, though he went limping to his grave. We read in the former chapter how Jacob had power with God, and prevailed; here we find what power he had with men too. Here is, I. A friendly meeting between Jacob and Esau, ver. 1-4. II. Their conference at their meeting. Their discourse is, (1.) About Jacob's family, ver. 5-7. (2.) About the present he had sent, ver. 8-11. (3.) About the progress of their journey, ver. 12-15. III. Jacob's settlement in Canaan, his house-ground, and altar, ver. 16-20.

glossa.text:
« I will appease him, » etc. These things are interposed by the writer. For it belongs not to a prudent man to uncover his art, and so to make himself suspected by those with whom he deals.

*((GREG. hom. 14, in Evang., tom. II.)) Mystically.* When Jacob returns to his own parents, etc., *as far as* that with inward sweetness we may lay hold of God.

« And behold a man, » etc. ((ISID. in Gen., tom. V.)) In this chiefly the image of the Lord's sacrament is figured, etc., *as far as* that it may no more be able to beget.

« By no means, he says, shall thy name be called Jacob, but, » etc. ((HIERON. in Q. Hebr. )) Josephus in the first book of the Antiquities, etc., *as far as* we are led rather by the authority of Scripture, and of the angel, or of God, who himself called him Israel, than by that of any secular eloquence.

« And Jacob called, » etc. That also which follows, « and he blessed him, and Jacob called the name of that place Phanuel, saying, » etc. In the Hebrew it is called « Phanuel, » that we may know it to be the same place which in the other volumes of Scripture, according to the Hebrews, is read *Phanuel.*

((GREG., lib. IV Moral., cap. 6.)) It is asked: since Truth says: « No man shall see my face; » And: « No man hath seen God at any time, » how does Jacob testify: « I saw the Lord face to face? » For human minds, the inward eye being purged, etc., *as far as* whence I Cor. XIII: « Then shall I know even as I am known. »

notes.text: The right — Regard my righteous cause.
Sentence — Judgment on my behalf. Come - From thy tribunal.

Proved — Or, searched or tried it, by many temptations and afflictions. Night - When mens minds being freed from the distraction of business, and from the society of men, they act more vigourously and freely, according to their several inclinations. Tried - As gold-smiths do metals. Nothing - Nothing of unrighteousness. Purposed - I have resolved, upon deliberation, as the word implies. Mouth - I am so far from practicing against Saul's life, as they charge me, that I will not wrong him so much as in a word.

Concerning — Observing the works of the men of this age, how wicked they are, I was resolved to take more care in ordering my own actions. By - By the help of thy blessed word. Paths - The customs and practices. Destroyer - Or, of the violent man: such as Saul, and his courtiers and soldiers.
By — By thy great power.

glossa.text: *The prayer of David.* ((CASS.)) The prayer belongs to the person of the Lord, the Church being joined to him, which is his body. *Hear, O Lord. ((Ibid.))* This psalm makes us attend to the true nature of his humanity. The prayer of Christ is an instruction of the faithful: as by weeping over Lazarus he taught us to have charity toward our neighbour; he fled his persecutors, that he might take from us the boldness of ill-considered rashness. First, he asks that it be rendered to him according to justice. *Not in deceitful lips.* As one who is unjustly condemned; or, as one who says: Lord, Lord, and does not do the works. ((AUG.)) Or, let my judgment come forth from thy countenance not in deceitful lips, so that in judging I may not put forth anything other than I understand.

*From thy countenance.* ((CASS.)) That is, according to those things which thou knowest in me, who have no sin. *Judgment.* Whereby he who was judged may be seen to have come forth as his own. *From thy countenance,* not from the disposition of the Jews, which deed is plain in the resurrection. Or, *judgment,* whereby he discerns all things.
*Thou hast proved.* ((CASS.)) From the likeness of a furnace, etc., *as far as* thou knowest me to be pure.

*Hard ways. ((Ibid.))* Namely the works of men: which, namely, the works of men deserve. Or, which men ought to imitate, for whom the road of the vices is easy, that of the virtues hard. Or, it was not found, so that he should not speak, that is, that I may not say these things boastfully, or, that I may not sin with my tongue, which is the work of men. ((AUG.)) Or, the hard ways of the thief, etc., *as far as* after I had gone along the hard ways and completed my steps.

*Perfect thou.* ((CASS.)) Even to the end: before that there is nothing but a beginning. Steps, that is, human actions, so that they who wish to imitate may not be moved away from thee, nor their footsteps from them.

*I have cried. ((Ibid.))* Secondly, he prays that his purity be delivered from the ambushes of the Jews. I too have cried, as though thou shouldst say, this belongs to none but the just man, who prays with confidence, because he knows he is heard.
*Make wonderful.* ((AUG.)) Wonderful are the things that are new: these are the things which he yielded in the flesh, the Jews marvelling.

notes.text: Because it lay quite wide of his design, which was this, to show that God's rejecting the Jews and receiving the gentiles was consistent with his word
Because such a doctrine would not only have had no tendency to convince, but would have evidently tended to harden, the Jews;

Because when he sums up his argument in the close of the chapter, he has not one word, or the least intimation, about it.

1. In Christ - This seems to imply an appeal to him. In the Holy Ghost - Through his grace.

2. I have great sorrow - A high degree of spiritual sorrow and of spiritual Joy may consist together, chap. viii, 39. By declaring his sorrow for the unbelieving Jews, who excluded themselves from all the blessings he had enumerated, he shows that what he was now about to speak, he did not speak from any prejudice to them.

3. I could wish - Human words cannot fully describe the motions of souls that are full of God. As if he had said, I could wish to suffer in their stead; yea, to be an anathema from Christ in their place. In how high a sense he wished this, who can tell, unless himself had been asked and had resolved the question? Certainly he did not then consider himself at all, but only others and the glory of God. The thing could not be; yet the wish was pious and solid; though with a tacit condition, if it were right and possible.

Whose is the adoption, &c. — He enumerates six prerogatives, of which the first pair respect God the Father, the second Christ, the third the Holy Ghost. The adoption and the glory - That is, Israel is the first-born child of God, and the God of glory is their God, Deut. iv, 7; Psalm cvi, 20. These are relative to each other. At once God is the Father of Israel, and Israel are the people of God. He speaks not here of the ark, or any corporeal thing. God himself is "the glory of his people Israel." And the covenants, and the giving of the law - The covenant was given long before the law. It is termed covenants, in the plural, because it was so often and so variously repeated, and because there were two dispositions of it, Gal. iv, 24, frequently called two covenants; the one promising, the other exhibiting the promise. And the worship, and the promises - The true way of worshipping God; and all the promises made to the fathers.

To the preceding, St. Paul now adds two more prerogatives. Theirs are the fathers — The patriarchs and holy men of old, yea, the Messiah himself. Who is over all, God blessed forever - The original words imply the self-existent, independent Being, who was, is, and is to come. Over all - The supreme; as being God, and consequently blessed forever. No words can more dearly express his divine, supreme majesty, and his gracious sovereignty both over Jews and, gentiles.

glossa.text:
*I speak the truth.* Now nothing can separate me, but once I was separated; whence now I grieve, and thus evils are now turned unto good.

*I speak the truth. ((AMBR.))* Because he seemed to speak against the Jews, etc., *as far as* yet Job was the fifth of the sons of Esau, namely from Abraham, that is, a grandson of Esau.

*For my brethren.* The Jews, or also for the drawing back of those who are now brethren in the faith, who are also my kinsmen: and so I sinned the more grievously.

 ((AUG.)) So perfect an eminence of the Son is here declared, etc., *as far as: The mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus ((I Tim. II))*.

notes.text:
Jesus withdrew into a desert place -

1. To avoid Herod:

2. Because of the multitude pressing upon him, Mark vi, xxxii, and

3. To talk with his disciples, newly returned from their progress, Luke ix, x, apart - From all but his disciples. John vi, 1.
The time is now past — The usual meal time. Mark vi, 35; Luke ix, 12.

glossa.text: *And when Jesus had heard it.* After among the Jews the law and the prophet lose their head and their voice: Jesus passes over to the desert place of the Church, which before had no husband. *He withdrew.* He did not flee out of fear, but he withdrew, sparing his enemies, lest they should join murder to murder, giving an example of rashness to be shunned. Or *he withdrew,* that he might prove the faith of them that believe; whence: *And when the crowds had heard,* etc. *On foot.* By their own labour, that they might show the ardour of their mind. They leave the cities, that is, their former ways of life. They have the will, but not the strength to arrive. Therefore Jesus goes out to meet them, and having pity heals them, that a full faith may have its reward at once. Behold how greatly he is delighted with the devotion of them that believe.

*And when it was evening,* etc. Jesus withdraws from Judea, goes into the desert, the crowds follow, whom he meets and heals. This not in the morning or at midday, but in the evening, when the sun of justice had set and the end of the world had drawn near.

*His disciples.* Carnal, and ignorant of the coming miracle of the refreshment, to whom it had been said: *Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles ((Matth. X))*.

Mystically. The Jews disdain that the Gentiles should be received, and they murmur: whose voice Isaias uses ((Isa. XL)): *Behold the nations are as a drop of a bucket.* Again: *All nations are as though they were not, but they are before him.* But the Lord determined to refresh them by the apostles; whence he subjoins: *But Jesus,* etc.

*Send away the crowds.* It is long that she has followed idols, and therefore she is not to be fed by us with the bread of the word of God.

*Give ye them.* He provokes them to give, that, when they testify that they have nothing, the greatness of the sign may be the better known; wherein he also hints that by them the hungry hearts are to be fed.

*Five loaves and two fishes.* By the five loaves and the two fishes the whole Old Testament is signified. By the five loaves, the five books of Moses, which are well of barley, which is the food of beasts of burden, for to the untaught things rough and coarse must be given. *For the sensual man perceiveth not the things that are of the spirit of God ((I Cor. I))* . Within, nevertheless, lies hidden the marrow of a most sweet meaning. By the two fishes, the prophets and the psalms: whence also after the resurrection he says: *The things that are written in the law and in very many prophets concerning me ((Luc. XXIV))* .

*Having taken the five,* etc. He took five loaves, he did not create new ones, because coming in the flesh he preached no other things than those which had been foretold, and fulfilled them in deed. *He blessed.* When, opening their understanding that they might understand the Scriptures, he multiplied them by the gift of an inward sweetness. He broke, when he brought forth the mysteries of the law into the midst.

*The fragments.* The more secret things, which cannot be grasped by the untaught, are not to be held negligently, but are to be diligently sought out by the twelve apostles, who are signified by the twelve baskets, and by their successors. With baskets servile works are carried on. *And the weak things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the strong ((I Cor. I))*.

*Besides women and children.* The frail sex and the lesser age are unworthy of the number. It signifies those weak in faith, not yet fit for battle.

VERS. 22. *And immediately he compelled,* etc. ((RAB.)) Who, as John says, *were about to come to make him king ((Joan. VI))*, who had seen the miracle of the loaves, etc., *as far as* let us pray for them, lest they soften us.

notes.text: Thirsteth — For the grace of God and the blessings of the gospel. This thirst implies a vehement, and active, and restless desire after it. No money - Those who are most worthless and wicked, if they do but thirst may be welcome. Buy - Procure or receive that which is freely offered. Wine and milk - All gospel-blessings; in particular, that peace and joy in the Holy Ghost, which are better than wine, and that love of God which nourishes the soul, as milk does the body.

Money — All your time, and strength, and cost. Not bread - For those things which can never nourish or satisfy you, such as worldly goods, or pleasures. Eat ye - That which is truly and solidly, and everlastingly good. In fatness - In this pleasant food of gospel-enjoyments.

An everlasting covenant — That everlasting covenant of grace and peace which I made with Abraham, and his seed. Of David - Even that covenant which was made first with Abraham, and then with David, concerning those glorious and sure blessings which God hath promised to his people, one and the chief of which was giving Christ to die for their sins. David here seems to be put for the son of David.

Behold — I have appointed, and will in due time actually give. Him - The David last mentioned, even Christ. A witness - To declare the will of God concerning the duty and salvation of men, to bear witness to truth, to confirm God's promises, and, among others, those which respect the calling of the Gentiles: to be a witness of both parties of that covenant made between God and men. The people - To all people.

Thou — Thou, O Messiah. Call - To the knowledge of thyself. Knewest not - With that special knowledge which implies approbation. Because - Because the Lord shall by many tokens, manifest himself to be thy God, and thee to be his son and faithful servant. Glorify thee - By confirming thy word with illustrious signs and miracles, and particularly by thy resurrection, and glorious ascension.

glossa.text:
*All you that thirst, come.* ((HIER.)) Because he had said that the vessel fashioned against the Church was to be broken, and every tongue armed against the knowledge of God to be overcome, he calls believers to the river of God, which is filled with waters.

*Eat ye.* By hearing, by speaking, by reading, by meditating, by working, by keeping in the heart. For the divine Scripture is both drink, when open, and food, when hidden. It is also both the water and the bread that came down from heaven.

*Why do you weigh out silver.* You weigh the sacred words, but not the refreshment. You who keep the appearance of the letter alone lose, from the spiritual understanding, the fatness of the inward refreshment.

*Behold, a witness.* He challenged the Jews to believe, but because he knew that, when they did not believe, the Gentiles were going to believe, he says that he has sent his Son to announce his precepts to the peoples.
*The Lord thy God.* ((ID.)) When he is called Father, the Father of Christ is called, according to the divinity, the Father of glory; according to the humanity, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

*Compassionate and merciful.* ((CAS.)) Thirdly he explains at greater length the things which in the second place he set forth briefly. As if: Deservedly in these things they shall praise, because *compassionate,* etc. The parts of praise are set down here which were set down above, but they cannot be explained one by one: for who could fully explain his works or his power? ((AUG.)) *Compassionate and merciful.* To those to whom he has given that pardon. *Patient.* To those to whom he has not yet given it, but waits that he may give it.

((CAS.)) *Tender mercies.* He begins from the works, that he may be called compassionate while he restores the fallen. *Merciful,* by nature, even while he creates. *Patient,* this he takes from the second topic of praise, namely from power, which he praises, not because he has hung the lands, restrained the seas, painted the heavens with stars, etc., but because he bears with sinners, that they may be converted. *And his tender mercies.* ((AUG.)) For if thou takest away thy evil works, and there remain in thee nothing but his works, his mercy will not let thee go: but if thou dost not let go thy own works, his severity will be upon thy works, when he shall say: *Go, ye cursed, into everlasting fire ((Matth. XXV))*.

lines: Jacob wrestled till daybreak by the river.
I will not let you go until you bless me.
He limped away with a new name and the dawn.
We come marked by the struggle, and blessed.
The crowd was hungry, and the disciples had nothing.
Jesus took the bread, gave thanks, and all were fed.
Come, let us worship the God who blesses and feeds.
We come hungry; bless us. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Smell the loaves and the fish broken open on a deserted hillside, five thousand fed from almost nothing.
In your hands, there is enough.
Jacob fought the stranger all night by the Jabbok, holding on through the dark, refusing to let go.
In your hands, there is enough.
He would not loose his grip until the blessing came — and it came, with a new name and a wound and the sunrise.
In your hands, there is enough.
Bring your empty baskets and your hungry hearts; Jesus takes the little we have, gives thanks, and it overflows.
In your hands, there is enough. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Jacob held on through the dark till the blessing came.
In your hands, there is enough.
He limped into the dawn with a new name.
In your hands, there is enough.
Jesus took five loaves, gave thanks, and all were fed.
In your hands, there is enough.
Come, let us worship the God who feeds us.
In your hands, there is enough. Amen.

turn.gravity: Jacob wrestles all night at the Jabbok and limps away blessed (Genesis 32); the Psalm cries out of hunger and want; Paul aches with grief for kin cut off from the promise (Romans 9); and Jesus — grieving John's death — turns from his own sorrow to feed a famished crowd from five loaves. The nerve: compassion answering scarcity in the wake of loss, not around it.
turn.trap: Becomes either a fundraising appeal ("give what little you have and watch it multiply") or a bare nature-miracle spectacle — missing that Jesus withdrew in grief first, and that the miracle grows out of sorrow, not showmanship.
turn.hinge: He feeds five thousand from nothing, but through the disciples' hands, not around them — the miracle needs their meager five loaves and the labor of carrying them out, basket by basket.

doors.claim: Even grieving his own loss, Jesus turns toward the crowd's hunger — the compassion is not despite the sorrow but issuing from it.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: He did not retire into the desert through fear of death, as some suppose, but in mercy to His enemies, that they might not add murder to murder.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He went out and saw a great multitude, and he had compassion upon them, and healed their sick.

doors.say: He was grieving when he saw the crowd's hunger — and grief did not close his hand, it opened it.
doors.do: Ask them to name one act of compassion they've withheld because they felt too depleted to give it, and give it anyway this week.

doors.landing: Through their hands, not around them
doors.claim: Christ multiplies through the disciples' offering and labor, not instead of it — the miracle needs what little they have and the work of carrying it out.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Wherein He calls the Apostles to breaking of bread, that the greatness of the miracle might be more evident by their testimony that they had none.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: Then the loaves are given to the Apostles, because through them the gifts of divine grace were to be rendered.

doors.say: He didn't multiply the bread and hand it out himself — he put it in their hands and sent them into the crowd.
doors.do: Have them identify the meager thing they've been holding back from ministry because it seemed too small to matter, and hand it over.

doors.claim: The twelve leftover baskets testify that nothing of Christ's provision is wasted or forgotten — abundance leaves a record.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: For this reason also He caused twelve baskets to remain over and above, that Judas might bear his basket.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Each of the Apostles fills his basket of the fragments left by his Saviour, that these fragments might witness that they were true loaves that were multiplied.

doors.say: Even the leftovers were gathered up — nothing Christ provides is thrown away, not even the excess.
doors.do: Have the congregation name one thing God provided that they let go to waste, and commit to gathering the fragments this time.

synthesis.convergence: Jacob limps away blessed after wrestling all night (Genesis 32); the crowd waits all day in the wilderness and is fed at evening; Paul aches with grief over kin estranged from the promise (Romans 9). Every reading meets people spent, hungry, or grieving and finds God meeting them there with abundance out of scarcity — through their exhaustion, not around it.
synthesis.claim: God does not wait for your strength to return before feeding you — bring what little you have, spent as you are, and watch it be enough.
synthesis.here: For a congregation running on empty — post-loss, post-crisis, depleted — don't ask them to muster more. Ask them to bring the five loaves they already have and hand it over.

turn.subtract: Three landings — grief turned to compassion, the disciples' hands, or the leftover witness. Choose the one your people most need; let the other two go.
